summaries.example: Imagine a fair coin tossed many times. The coin tosses may be a chance process: each toss has a physical possibility of heads or tails. But the row of results might look very regular, such as heads every time. A chance process does not guarantee that every result-pattern will look random.
summaries.summary: Chance and randomness are closely related ideas, but they are not simply identical. Chance concerns the physical setup or process that can produce different outcomes. For example, a coin may have a chance of landing heads because of how it is tossed. Randomness often concerns the resulting collection of outcomes: whether it lacks a useful pattern, is difficult to compress into a short rule, or represents a larger group fairly. These ideas can come apart. A chance process can produce a very unusual sequence, and a rule-governed process can produce a sequence that looks random. The same distinction helps explain why random sampling can work even when the method used to choose people is not itself a chance process. The entry also separates randomness from determinism and unpredictability. Something may be unpredictable because we do not know enough, without being undetermined. The main lesson is that chance and randomness overlap in many ordinary examples, but they should be examined separately.
key_ideas: People often use “chance” and “randomness” as if they mean the same thing, but philosophers distinguish them.
Chance usually belongs to the process that produces an outcome. Randomness often describes the group or sequence of outcomes.
A chance process can produce an unusual or orderly sequence by accident.
A sequence can look random even when a rule, rather than chance, produced it.
Randomness can help us notice when a process needs more explanation, but it is not proof that chance caused it.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use these ideas when judging games, experiments, statistics, and scientific explanations. If we confuse chance with randomness, we may think every chance result must look mixed or messy, or that every random-looking result was caused by chance. Keeping the ideas apart helps us reason more carefully about evidence and predictions.

important_terms.definition: A physical possibility or likelihood connected with how a process works, not merely with what someone believes.
A lack of an obvious, useful pattern in a group or sequence of results.
A process in which earlier conditions completely fix what happens next.
Being unable to know ahead of time exactly what will happen.

questions_to_think_about: Can a fair spinner land on the same color many times by chance?
Is something random if it is hard to predict but follows a hidden rule?
Why might a random-looking sample be useful for learning about a larger group?
Are chance and unpredictability always the same?

summaries.example: Suppose a computer uses the time on its clock as a starting value, or seed, for a pseudorandom-number program. The resulting digits may pass several statistical tests and look random. Yet the sequence is generated by a definite algorithm from a finite seed, so it is compressible in principle rather than algorithmically random. If the start time was selected by chance, the output may have a chance-related origin without itself being random in the stronger product sense.
summaries.summary: The entry investigates whether chance and randomness are the same or systematically connected. It distinguishes objective chance from subjective belief and treats chance primarily as a feature of a physical process or trial. A coin toss, for instance, may have a single-case chance even if no other toss occurs. Randomness, by contrast, is developed mainly as a property of a product: a finite or infinite sequence that is disorderly, unpatterned, statistically typical, or not effectively compressible. Algorithmic approaches, including Martin-Löf testing and Kolmogorov complexity, provide rigorous working notions, though the entry notes that no single definition settles every intuitive use of “random.” The proposed Commonplace Thesis—roughly, that what happens by chance is random—can be refined using hypothetical repeated trials, but counterexamples remain. A chancy process may produce a biased or dependent sequence, an exceptionally short sequence, or an outcome that becomes certain after earlier results. Conversely, deterministic chaotic dynamics may generate random-looking sequences, while indeterministic classical systems may lack any objective probability distribution. Alternative theories try to connect chance and randomness more closely, but often do so by building one notion into the other or by changing its meaning. The conclusion is that chance and randomness overlap and provide evidence about one another, yet they are separate concepts.
key_ideas: Objective chance is a process notion: it concerns the physical setup, laws, and causal conditions that produce an outcome, including possible single-case chances.
Product randomness is a sequence notion. Mathematical accounts include passing effective statistical tests and resisting useful compression.
The Commonplace Thesis is attractive but fails in important cases. Chancy processes may yield biased, dependent, short, or otherwise unrepresentative sequences.
Conversely, deterministic chaotic systems can generate sequences with random-looking statistical behavior, while classical indeterministic systems need not supply a probability distribution.
Random sampling need not be produced by a chance mechanism. What matters may be that the sample is representative and not predictably biased with respect to relevant population features.
Determinism, chance, and unpredictability are distinct. A deterministic system can be unpredictable to limited observers, and indeterminism alone does not guarantee objective chance.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction affects how we interpret probability, statistical inference, scientific explanation, and physical theories. A random sample can be useful without being selected by genuine chance; a random-looking pattern can arise from a deterministic mechanism; and a chancy outcome need not be part of a random-looking sequence. Understanding these cases prevents us from treating appearance, unpredictability, and physical probability as interchangeable.

important_terms.definition: A mind-independent physical probability associated with a process or trial, rather than a person’s confidence or evidence.
Randomness treated as a feature of a sequence or collection of outcomes, such as disorder or incompressibility.
Randomness treated as a feature of the process generating an outcome; in the entry, this is often identified with a chance process.
The thesis that an outcome happens by chance exactly when it is random, or belongs to a suitable random sequence.
A sequence is algorithmically random when it cannot be effectively singled out as exceptional or described substantially more briefly than it is.
A system is deterministic when its laws and complete state at one time fix its state at other times.
A process or outcome cannot be reliably predicted from the information and theory available to an agent.
A sequence produced by a rule that can imitate many statistical features of randomness without being genuinely random.

questions_to_think_about: If a fair coin produces an unusually biased finite sequence, should that sequence count as random?
Does observing an algorithmically random-looking sequence justify believing that its generating process involved objective chance?
Can a deterministic chaotic system be random in a scientifically useful sense?
What should determine the relevant reference class for assigning a chance to an event?
Would a theory of chance based on frequencies work for a single event or a process with very few trials?

summaries.example: A school wants to learn about students’ favorite lunch. It chooses students whose birth-minute ends in 7. The choosing rule is not a chance mechanism, because the rule is fixed. Still, if birth-minute endings are unrelated to lunch preferences, the sample might represent the school fairly and function as a random sample. This shows that useful randomness in a sample need not come from a chance process.
summaries.summary: The entry examines a common assumption: that an event is random exactly when it happens by chance. It argues that this assumption hides an important difference. Objective chance is usually attached to a physical process, such as a coin toss, radioactive decay, or another trial with several physically possible outcomes. Randomness is often attached to the product of a process—a sequence or sample—and concerns features such as disorder, lack of exploitable pattern, typicality, or incompressibility. This difference creates problems for the Commonplace Thesis. A fair process can happen to produce an unusual sequence, while a biased or history-dependent process can produce outcomes by chance without producing a random-looking sequence. Randomness and chance can also separate in the other direction: deterministic chaotic systems can be very difficult to predict and can generate sequences with the statistical appearance of randomness. The entry discusses mathematical approaches to randomness, including tests for exceptional sequences and the idea that random sequences cannot be effectively compressed. It also explains why unpredictability should not be confused with indeterminism. In the end, randomness is useful evidence about a process, but the two concepts are not identical.
key_ideas: Chance and randomness are connected, but they answer different questions: how a result was produced versus how a collection of results looks or behaves.
A single event can have objective chance even when there are no repeated trials to measure.
Mathematical theories of random sequences look for properties such as balanced frequencies, absence of exploitable patterns, and resistance to compression.
A chance process can produce an odd sequence, especially when outcomes are biased or depend on previous outcomes.
A deterministic process, especially a chaotic one, can produce outcomes that are hard to predict and resemble a random sequence.
The entry concludes that randomness can be evidence for chance, but it does not prove that chance was involved.
summaries.why_it_matters: These distinctions matter whenever we use data to make claims. Statistical methods often depend on representative samples, not necessarily on a physically chancy selection method. Likewise, a pattern that looks random may result from a deterministic rule, while an unusual result may still have occurred by chance. Careful reasoning requires asking whether we are describing the process, the data it produces, or our own limits as observers.

important_terms.definition: A physical probability belonging to a process, not simply a person’s confidence that an event will happen.
A feature of a set or sequence of results: it has no useful pattern, is not predictably biased, or is difficult to describe briefly.
The idea that events happening by chance and random outcomes are exactly the same thing.
A process in which the laws and starting state fix the later state, even if people cannot calculate it.
The difficulty of forecasting an outcome; it may result from limited knowledge rather than from chance.
A sequence made by a rule that can look random in ordinary tests but is not random in the strongest mathematical sense.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a sequence with alternating heads and tails fail to be random even though it has equal numbers of each?
Can an outcome be unpredictable without being random?
Why does choosing a sample by a fixed rule sometimes still give reliable statistical information?
If earlier results change later probabilities, can all the results together be random?
What evidence would make you think a random-looking sequence came from chance?
